clinicalPearls: A locally aggressive dermal spindle-cell sarcoma of intermediate malignancy with a strong tendency to recur locally but a low rate of metastasis
Presents as a slowly enlarging, indurated plaque or nodule, often on the trunk or proximal limbs of young to middle-aged adults
Early lesions may be mistaken for a scar, keloid or benign dermatofibroma, delaying diagnosis
Driven by a COL1A1-PDGFB gene fusion, usually from a supernumerary ring chromosome, leading to constitutive PDGF receptor signalling
Histology shows a uniform storiform (cartwheel) arrangement of spindle cells that are diffusely CD34-positive and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern
The infiltrative tentacle-like growth extends well beyond the clinical margin, explaining the high local recurrence rate with inadequate excision
Wide local excision with clear margins or Mohs micrographic surgery is standard, with imatinib available for unresectable, recurrent or metastatic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a dermal and subcutaneous fibroblastic tumour of intermediate malignancy characterised by a COL1A1-PDGFB gene fusion, typically carried on a supernumerary ring chromosome derived from chromosomes 17 and 22. The fusion places platelet-derived growth factor B under the control of the collagen COL1A1 promoter, resulting in continuous autocrine PDGF receptor beta activation and tumour cell proliferation. The tumour grows as a storiform proliferation of CD34-positive spindle cells that infiltrates the dermis and subcutis in an insidious, finger-like fashion far beyond the visible lesion. A high-grade fibrosarcomatous transformation can occur, conferring greater metastatic risk.
additionalInvestigations: MRI to define the depth and extent of the tumour before wide excision
Skin biopsy with histological assessment of storiform architecture and fat infiltration
CD34 immunohistochemistry, typically diffusely positive, aiding distinction from dermatofibroma
Molecular testing for the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion in ambiguous cases
Histological search for fibrosarcomatous transformation, which alters prognosis
redFlags: Rapid growth or nodularity within a long-standing plaque suggesting fibrosarcomatous transformation
Recurrent lesion after previous inadequate excision
Deep fixation to underlying fascia, muscle or bone
Metastatic disease, which is uncommon but more likely with high-grade transformation
reference.prognosis: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans has an excellent prognosis when excised with adequate margins, but it recurs locally at high rates if margins are inadequate because of its infiltrative growth. Metastasis is rare and occurs mainly with fibrosarcomatous transformation.
pitfalls: Underestimating the infiltrative extent and taking inadequate margins, leading to recurrence
Mistaking it for a benign dermatofibroma, keloid or scar and delaying treatment
Failing to consider targeted PDGFR inhibition for unresectable or metastatic disease

management: For localized disease, surgery is the primary and usually the only treatment needed; elective lymph node dissection is not indicated since nodal spread is rare
Wide local excision with a generous margin (most series describe a minimum of about 3 cm, including underlying fascia) is a standard first line approach

Mohs micrographic surgery is an alternative first line option, particularly for tissue conservation at cosmetically or functionally sensitive sites, with comparable or lower local recurrence than wide excision
Recurrence risk tracks with margin adequacy; positive or narrow margins should prompt re-excision when feasible

Radiation therapy can be used selectively as an adjunct or alternative when adequate surgical margins cannot be achieved or resection would cause major functional or cosmetic deficit; no specific dose regimen is asserted here

For locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic disease, a PDGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib) has the clearest documented activity, reflecting the COL1A1-PDGFB driver fusion present in most tumors
Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy has only limited supporting data in this disease and should be considered a fallback rather than a preferred systemic option
Advanced or unresectable disease should be managed by a multidisciplinary team including surgical oncology, radiation oncology, and medical oncology

The fibrosarcomatous variant follows a more aggressive course; treatment still centers on adequate surgical excision but warrants closer follow-up and earlier consideration of systemic options if disease becomes unresectable or metastatic

Follow-up should include regular clinical examination of the surgical site and region for an extended period, with vigilance concentrated in the first several years, since most recurrences occur within this window
Refer to a center with Mohs expertise or a multidisciplinary sarcoma or skin oncology team whenever clear margins cannot be obtained or excision would risk major functional or cosmetic compromise
Refer locally advanced, unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic disease to medical oncology for consideration of PDGFR-targeted therapy alongside multidisciplinary surgical and radiation planning
